prompts.L5:
Please write a text about the following topic:

Keywords: The, And, Rough

outputs.L1:
The dim sea glints chill. The white sun is shy,  
And the skeleton weeds and the never-dry,  
Rough, long grasses keep white with frost  
At the hilltop by the finger-post;  
The smoke of the traveller’s-joy is puffed  
Over hawthorn berry and hazel tuft.  

I read the sign. Which way shall I go?  
A voice says: “You would not have doubted so  
At twenty.” Another voice, gentle with scorn,  
Says: “At twenty you wished you had never been born.”  

One hazel lost a leaf of gold  
From a tuft at the tip, when the first voice told  
The other he wished to know what ’twould be  
To be sixty by this same post. “You shall see,”  
He laughed—and I had to join his laughter—  
“You shall see; but either before or after,  
Whatever happens, it must befall,  
A mouthful of earth to remedy all  
Regrets and wishes shall freely be given;  
And if there be a flaw in that heaven,  
’Twill be freedom to wish, and your wish may be  
To be here or anywhere talking to me,  
No matter what the weather, on earth,  
At any age between death and birth,  
To see what day or night can be,  
The sun and the frost, the land and the sea,  
Summer, Autumn, Winter, Spring,—  
With a poor man of any sort, down to a king,  
Standing upright out in the air,  
Wondering where he shall journey, O where?”
outputs.L2:
The darkened ocean gives off a cold shimmer. A pale sun hangs back, almost hidden.  
At the hill’s summit, beside the signpost, bare weeds and coarse, tall grasses that never seem fully dry are whitened by frost.  
The traveller’s-joy sends its smoky fluff drifting above the hawthorn berries and the hazel clumps.

I look at the words on the sign and wonder which road to take.  
One inner voice tells me that, when I was twenty, I would not have hesitated like this.  
Another voice, mild but mocking, answers that at twenty I had wanted not to be alive at all.

From the end of one hazel spray, a single golden leaf fell  
just as the first voice confessed to the other that he wanted to know  
what it would be like to stand at this same signpost at sixty.  
“You will find out,” the other laughed, and I could not help laughing too.  
“You will find out. But sooner or later, whatever else occurs,  
a little earth in the mouth will come as the cure for every regret and longing.  
And if that heaven has any imperfection, it will be this:  
that one may still be free to desire, and perhaps your desire will be  
to stand here—or somewhere else—speaking with me,  
in any weather upon the earth,  
at any age between birth and death,  
watching what day and night can offer:  
sunlight and frost, countryside and sea,  
summer, autumn, winter, spring—  
with any kind of poor man, even one as high as a king,  
standing upright in the open air,  
asking himself where he should travel next, and where.”
outputs.L3:
The speaker stands at a cold, frosty crossroads on a hilltop, surrounded by a stark but beautiful landscape. From this high place, they can see the sea in the distance, the rising or setting sun, the plants touched by frost, and the signpost marking different possible paths. The scene is both physical and symbolic: the crossroads represents a moment of decision, while the wintry setting suggests age, stillness, and reflection.

Faced with the choice of which road to take, the speaker feels uncertain. This uncertainty leads to an inward conversation, as different voices within the speaker begin to reflect on the passage of time, the nature of choice, and the relationship between youth and age. The speaker wonders whether life would have felt simpler or more decisive in youth, when energy and confidence might have made choices seem easier.

One inner voice suggests that, at twenty, the speaker would not have hesitated so much. Youth is imagined as a time of boldness, when a person might choose a path quickly and move forward without being troubled by doubt. However, another voice challenges this idealized view of youth by remembering the despair and confusion felt at that age. The poem therefore refuses to present either youth or age as entirely free from uncertainty. Each stage of life has its own burdens: youth may suffer from intensity and hopelessness, while age may suffer from hesitation and regret.

The poem develops a contrast between wishes and regrets throughout life. At different ages, people long for what they do not have: the young may wish for escape, certainty, or a future transformed, while the old may regret lost opportunities or yearn for the vitality of earlier years. Human life is shown as a continual movement between desire and dissatisfaction. Yet the poem suggests that death ultimately brings an end to these conflicts. In death, all wishes and regrets are resolved or silenced, since the struggles of choice, longing, and disappointment belong to earthly life.

In its final imaginative turn, the speaker considers the possibility of an afterlife. Even there, if the soul retained the freedom to wish, it might not desire perfect certainty or eternal peace. Instead, it might long to return to the earthly experience of standing at a crossroads, surrounded by frost, sunlight, sea, and living plants, feeling the wonder and uncertainty of being alive. The poem therefore suggests that doubt itself, though painful, is part of life’s beauty. The very moments that trouble us may later seem precious, because they contain the mystery, freedom, and possibility of human existence.
outputs.L4:
At a frosty crossroads beside the sea, the speaker pauses before two possible paths and turns the moment into a meditation on life, choice, and mortality. The cold landscape, the open water, and the branching road create a scene of uncertainty: the speaker is not only deciding where to walk, but also reflecting on the larger question of how a human life is shaped by decisions, doubts, and regrets. To explore these feelings, the poem imagines a dialogue between two versions of the self—the younger self, still full of longing and possibility, and the older self, who looks back with the knowledge that every choice leaves something behind.

Through this conversation, the poem examines the pain of wanting many different lives at once. The speaker longs for certainty, yet recognizes that certainty may be impossible while one is alive. Every path promises something, but also demands a sacrifice. The younger self wants to know which way will lead to fulfillment, while the older self understands that no life can contain every wish. This tension gives the poem much of its emotional force: it presents human existence as a series of crossroads where one must choose without ever fully knowing what the choice will mean.

The poem also connects this uncertainty to the thought of death. Death appears as the one condition that might finally end desire, doubt, and regret. In death, all wishes may be resolved simply because wishing itself comes to an end. Yet the poem does not treat this as a comforting solution. Instead, it suggests that what seems like peace may also be a loss. To be free from uncertainty would mean being free from the very experiences that make life human: hesitation, curiosity, longing, and the hope that another path might still be possible.

By the end, the poem imagines the greatest freedom not as escape from life, but as the ability to return to it. The speaker dreams of coming back to ordinary earthly moments—the cold air, the sea, the crossroads, the unfinished act of choosing. These simple experiences become precious because they belong to a world where nothing is fully settled. The poem ultimately finds meaning not in perfect answers, but in the act of wondering itself. Human life is valuable precisely because it is uncertain, because it asks us to desire, to doubt, to choose, and to continue standing before the unknown.
outputs.L5:
**The Rough Path**

The wind moved across the hills, and the sky grew darker with every passing minute. The road ahead was rough, full of stones, mud, and deep tracks left by old wagons. Still, the traveler continued, holding tightly to his coat and keeping his eyes on the distant light.

The journey was not easy, and every step required patience. His boots slipped, his hands grew cold, and the rough ground seemed to stretch on forever. But he knew that difficult paths often led to meaningful places.

At last, he reached the top of the hill. The clouds began to open, and a soft golden light touched the land below. The road had been rough, and the journey had been long, but the view made every hardship worthwhile.

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a poem in the style of Edward Thomas about standing at a frosty crossroads near the sea, reflecting on age, regret, death, and the choice of which road to take.
counterfactuals.output:
At dawn I stood where four white roads  
Were bitten pale with rime,  
And heard, beyond the blackthorn hedge,  
The sea keep ancient time.

No gull was up. The fields lay still,  
Their grasses stiff as wire;  
A gate, half open, held one star  
Like a forgotten fire.

Behind me, lanes I knew too well  
Went back by fold and farm,  
By rooms where words were left unsaid  
And bread was never warm.

Before me, one road dipped to where  
The shingle took the foam;  
One climbed inland among the elms  
That never called me home.

Another, narrow, lost itself  
In thorn and frozen sedge;  
The last went straight, as if it knew  
The grave beyond the hedge.

I thought of age: not weight, but sound—  
A footstep heard too late;  
Of friends gone on before the frost,  
And one unlatched, dark gate.

Regret came quietly as breath  
Upon the morning air,  
Not crying out, but silvering  
The grass that had been bare.

What road was right? The sea replied  
By drawing back once more,  
And leaving every stone distinct,  
And nothing on the shore.

So long I stood, the sun at last  
Made red the eastern cloud;  
A robin sang from somewhere near,  
Too small, too clear, too loud.

Then, with no wisdom but the cold  
That counselled me to move,  
I took the road whose whiteness bore  
No sign of hate or love.

And as I went, the crossroads stayed  
Behind me in the light—  
Four ways, one frost, the sound of waves,  
And day not yet from night.
counterfactuals.label: cf_1

counterfactuals.prompt: Compose a melancholy early-20th-century English pastoral poem featuring a finger-post, winter grasses, hawthorn, hazel, and an internal dialogue between the speaker at twenty and sixty.
counterfactuals.output:
**At the Finger-Post**

The finger-post leans where the four roads part,  
Grey with the weather, green under rain;  
Its names are blotted about the heart,  
Yet one road leads to the hills again.  

Winter grasses, as thin as hair,  
Whisper and whiten along the ditch;  
The hawthorn stands in the bitter air,  
A thorny beggar, ragged and rich.  

Under the hazel the dead leaves keep  
Their small brown secrets from frost and sky;  
The fields lie folded as though in sleep,  
And only the rooks go travelling by.  

There I met him—myself at twenty—  
Light in the heel and quick in the breath;  
His pockets were poor, but his mornings plenty,  
And he had not yet made friends with death.  

“Which way, old man?” he cried, and started  
To see my face in the wind’s pale glass.  
“The left is for lovers, the right for the market,  
The straight road runs where the soldiers pass.”  

I answered him, “Lad, take none for certain;  
The sign-board lies, and the mile-stones dream.  
There is no road beyond the curtain  
But the one you choose by the failing gleam.”  

He laughed: “At sixty, the blood grows civil;  
You warm your hands at a vanished fire.  
I’ll follow the lark, and outface the devil,  
And come to the end of my own desire.”  

“Desire,” said I, “is a leaf in winter,  
Brown on the bough, then lost in the clay;  
Yet even its falling can scarcely splinter  
The silence that gathers at close of day.”  

The hazel clicked in the frost behind us,  
The hawthorn creaked like an old gate-bar;  
And the long white grasses seemed to remind us  
How far the near things, how near the far.  

He turned to the road where the dawn was lying,  
I stayed with the dusk and the finger-post;  
Between us went the wild geese crying—  
A living sound, and almost a ghost.  

O twenty, with all your roads before you,  
O sixty, with all your roads behind,  
The same cold heaven is bending o’er you,  
The same small thorn is pricking the wind.  

And still, when winter fields are hollow,  
And no man passes, and no birds sing,  
The finger-post points where I cannot follow,  
To April’s dust, and the ghost of spring.
counterfactuals.label: cf_2

counterfactuals.prompt: Generate a poem that imitates Edward Thomas’s “The Sign-Post,” preserving its rural imagery, reflective tone, and themes of mortality, memory, and indecision.
counterfactuals.output:
**The Mile-Stone**

Beside the lane the mile-stone leaned,  
Half sunk in grass and rain,  
And pointed, with a hand unseen,  
To village, wood, and plain.  

The blackbird from the hazel hedge  
Let fall a broken song;  
Beyond the stile the cart-ruts led  
Where I had meant to go along.  

But one road dipped by elder trees  
And one climbed bare to sky,  
And both were quiet in the breeze  
As if no feet passed by.  

I stood and read the lichened name  
Of towns I once had known;  
They stirred in me like winter flame,  
Then left me more alone.  

For every turning seemed to keep  
Some face, some day, some door,  
And every hollow, dark and deep,  
The footsteps gone before.  

The cattle moved without a sound  
Across the evening hill;  
The dead leaves gathered on the ground  
And all the air grew still.  

I thought: perhaps the way is best  
That asks no question where,  
But goes on fading with the west  
Through fields of empty air.  

Yet still I stayed. The mile-stone’s hand  
Pointed, and did not speak;  
The sun went down behind the land,  
The road grew white and bleak.  

Then from the farm a lantern shone,  
Small as a memory;  
I took the path that led me on—  
Or else it carried me.
counterfactuals.label: cf_3

counterfactuals.prompt: Can you write a Georgian-era nature poem where the narrator reads a signpost on a hilltop and hears two voices debating youth, old age, wishes, and the consolation of death?
counterfactuals.output:
**The Signpost on the Hill**

Upon the windy hill I stood,  
Where beeches bowed above the lane,  
And all the fields were washed with gold  
After a little rain.  

The sheep-bells tinkled in the combe,  
The lark went up with silver string;  
And on a post, against the sky,  
I read this weathered thing:  

**TO YOUTH: THE VALLEY AND THE ROSE.**  
**TO AGE: THE HEARTH AND WESTWARD LIGHT.**  
**TO WISHES: ROADS THAT NEVER CLOSE.**  
**TO DEATH: THE INN THAT KEEPS THE NIGHT.**  

I smiled to see such counsel writ  
By some old hand, long turned to clay;  
When from the grass, or from the air,  
Two voices crossed the day.  

The first cried, “Youth is all the world:  
The hawthorn milk, the river’s run,  
The warm cheek and the racing blood,  
The morning and the sun.  

“What care has youth for westward light,  
For settled chair or ashen log?  
Give me the path beyond the stile,  
The dew, the star, the dog;  

“Give me a wish, and I will make  
A ladder of it to the moon;  
Give me a wound, and I will sing  
And call the healing soon.  

“Death is a tale for winter mouths,  
A black rook on a distant tree;  
While May is loud in every hedge,  
What has the grave to do with me?”  

Then spoke the second, low and clear,  
Like water under frozen stone:  
“Youth has the rose, but not the root;  
Age has the root alone.  

“I too have run where skylarks run,  
And loved the rain upon my face;  
But every road that climbs the hill  
Comes down to one still place.  

“The wishes that you fling like seed  
Will flower, some, and some will fail;  
And those that bloom may bend your heart  
More sharply than the hail.  

“For longing is a travelling wind:  
It enters singing at the door,  
It shakes the candle of the soul,  
And leaves us wishing more.  

“But age can sit beside the fire  
And hear, within the ember’s glow,  
Not only what the heart desired,  
But why it hungered so.  

“And death—do not affront that word;  
It is no thief with lifted knife,  
But one who, when the lamp burns low,  
Draws close the book of life.  

“It lays the tired traveller down  
Where no more milestones vex the feet,  
And folds the hands that grasped at stars  
In darkness, kind and sweet.”  

“Kind?” cried the first. “Call silence kind?  
Call empty fields a promised bed?  
I would be bruised by all the world  
Before I would be dead.  

“Better the thorn that proves the rose,  
Better the rain that stings the cheek,  
Better the hunger of desire  
Than peace too dumb to speak.”  

The old voice answered, “Peace may be  
The speech for which we find no breath;  
And all our broken names for God  
May ripen into death.  

“Youth sees the blossom and believes  
The orchard made for one bright hour;  
Age sees the fruit, the fallen leaf,  
The patience of the flower.  

“So wish, young heart, but do not curse  
The hand that stills the fevered will;  
The road is good, the inn is good,  
And both are on the hill.”  

The lark had vanished into light,  
The sheep were shadows on the grass;  
The signpost creaked, and from the west  
I felt the evening pass.  

I read once more the weathered words,  
Then took the downward path again;  
And in my heart went youth and age  
Like sunlight after rain.
counterfactuals.label: cf_4

counterfactuals.prompt: Produce a rhymed literary poem set in a cold coastal landscape with frost, weeds, berries, and a traveller wondering which way to go while contemplating life “between death and birth.”
counterfactuals.output:
Along the coast where iron waters heave,  
And frost has stitched the grasses to the earth,  
A traveller stood at the edge of eve,  
And weighed the road between death and birth.  

The weeds leaned black from the frozen sand,  
Their brittle fingers combing at the air;  
Red berries burned in a thorny hand,  
Like little hearts left beating there.  

Behind him: fields where the year lay still,  
Before him: cliffs and the gulls’ grey cries;  
One path climbed toward the wind-stripped hill,  
One vanished where the tide would rise.  

He asked the foam, “Which way is mine?”  
The sea replied with a shattering breath;  
The frost made stars of the bramble vine,  
The berries glowed like drops of death.  

Yet in that cold, some hidden worth  
Stirred under root and rock and loam;  
For all our wandering on the earth  
Is loss and longing, wound and home.  

So there he lingered, dusk grown deep,  
With salt on his lips and ice in his hair,  
While under the weeds the seeds lay asleep,  
Dreaming of light in the winter air.  

And still he heard, through the surf’s dim mirth,  
A question no living soul can know:  
What is this life between death and birth—  
And which way now, in the dark, to go?
counterfactuals.label: cf_5
